questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, and profound generalized weakness. He had no significant medical history. He denied alcohol drinking or drug use. He had returned from a 2-week trip to India. He reported a lot of flooding in the local village where he stayed. He also had a lot of mosquito bites and had eaten different local delicacies bought from the streets. Two of his roommates had become sick with fever and vomiting prior to his return. He had not taken any pretravel advice. On examination, his temperature was 40.1°C, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/minute, and respiratory rate 24 breaths/minute. He had icteric sclerae and muscle tenderness in his lower back and bilateral calves. Investigations: Total white cell count 12 ×109/L Platelet count 145,000/μ L Hemoglobin 10 g/dL Aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L Alanine aminotransferase 190 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L Total bilirubin 15 mg/dL (predominantly conjugated) An ultrasound of the abdomen showed normal gallbladder and liver.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely route of acquisition of his illness?
questions.explanation: Floodwater exposure Although the differential diagnoses for his clinical presentation are broad (and hence must be ruled out carefully), the most likely diagnosis is leptospirosis. The following clues in his history and exam point to this diagnosis: jaundice, calf tenderness, and the elevated total bilirubin that is out of proportion to the mildly elevated aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels (rarely >200 U/L). Note that acute hepatitis A (from contaminated food consumption) presents similarly except for the profoundly elevated aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q29

questions.stem: A 23-year old soldier presented with a 2-day history of sudden onset fever, marked prostration, cough with bloody sputum, and shortness of breath. He was previously well and did not take any regular medications. On examination, his respiratory rate was 38 breaths/ minute, his oxygen saturations were 84% on room air, and his blood pressure was 86/42 mmHg. There was no neck stiffness and no rash. Investigations: Total white cell count 21 ×109/L Platelet count 72,000/μL CXR: widespread pulmonary infiltrates throughout the lung fields Twenty other soldiers had also presented with similar complaints in the last week. Bioterrorism via an aerosol route was suspected with onward person-to-person transmission.
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Yersinia pestis The pneumonic form of plague, caused by Yersinia pestis infection, occurs via inhalation of aerosols from an infected person (i.e., during close contact with a person). Person-toperson transmission does not occur in Q fever, tularemia, or anthrax and is exceedingly rare in brucellosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q28

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of general malaise, high temperatures, and prostration. She returned from a holiday in Malaysia 2 weeks ago, where she spent one week on a multi-adventure trip including forest hiking, zip lining, lake kayaking, and snorkeling in the sea. On examination, her temperature was 39°C, she was jaundiced, pale, and obtunded. Investigations: Total white cell count 3.2 ×109/L Neutrophils 2.2 ×109/L Hemoglobin 120 g/L Platelets 227 ×109/L Na 128 mmol/L (135–145) K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5–5) Urea 9 mmol/L (2.5–6.7) Creatinine 2.7 mg/dL (0.7–1.2) ALT 350 IU/L AST 247 IU/L Bilirubin 30 μmol/L (3–17) CXR: multiple lung infiltrates Blood cultures on admission negative HIV , hepatitis A + B + C, EBV , and CMV serology negative She was transferred to the intensive care unit where she required hemofiltration.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis The case describes a presentation of leptospirosis (Weil´s disease) with fever, acute kidney injury, and hepatitis following exposure to fresh water in the state with the highest incidence of this disease. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by serology. MAT is one of the most widely used essays. Severe leptospirosis is often treated with IV beta-lactam agents such as penicillin or ceftriaxone; milder cases can be managed with oral doxycycline. Tularemia is unlikely in this clinical scenario given the 10–12-day incubation period (3–5 days is more common for tularemia), and it is not known to be present in Malaysia. It is only seen in the northern hemisphere; cases in the United States are most commonly reported from Arkansas, Missouri, South Dakota, and Oklahoma. It is endemic in most European countries, China, and Japan. iGAS would be in the differential diagnosis; however, no clues are given in the question to lead you to this diagnosis (prior sore throat, signs/symptoms of skin/soft tissue infection). CCHF is not yet reported in Malaysia, although it has been reported from over 30 countries in Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and Europe. The incubation period, clinical features, and lab would be a good explanation otherwise. Acute hepatitis E may cause a fulminant infection with acute hepatic failure and encephalopathy in a small proportion of individuals, but there are usually risk factors such as pregnancy, malnourishment or preexisting liver disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q27

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of headache, myalgia, and fatigue. She had no recent travel, but she had competed in a triathlon 5 days prior. Investigations: AST 80 U/L (reference range: 10–40 U/L) ALT 120 U/L (reference range: 7–56 U/L) Urine dipstick: 3+ hematuria
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate test?
questions.explanation: Leptospira culture of blood Leptospira culture of blood and/or CSF should be performed during the first week of symptoms. After the first 7–10 days of symptoms, Leptospira culture of urine is preferred. Leptospira does not grow on routine bacterial culture media. For Leptospira serologic testing, only IgM should be tested, but it is insensitive during the first 7–10 days of illness.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q1

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of fever, headache, rigors, and myalgia. He lived in a rural area and recalled that he cleared a rat infestation in his house basement 2 weeks previously. On examination, he had hepatomegaly and conjunctival suffusion. Investigations: ALT 94 U/L CRP 124 mg/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae Leptospirosis is typically transmitted by contact with water or soil contaminated with animal urine. It is classically described as a biphasic illness with leptospiremic and leptospiuric phases. Acute renal failure and hepatitis are common complications in the context of leptospirosis; diagnosis is usually confirmed by serology. The other pathogens are all potentially acquired by exposure to rodents but leptospirosis is by far the commonest.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q27

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man returned from a 4-week volunteering expedition in the slums of Mumbai. He had been fully vaccinated prior to travel but had not taken any malaria prophylaxis. One week after his return he developed sudden onset fever, rigors, myalgia, and headache. On examination, his temperature was 38.1°C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/55 mmHg. He was alert and oriented, and there was no neck stiffness or photophobia. There was no rash or lymphadenopathy. He had profound tenderness of the calf muscles and paraspinal muscles bilaterally, and bilateral conjunctival suffusion. Examination of his cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal systems was unremarkable. Investigations: Neutrophils 8.5 ×109/L (1.5–7.0) Platelets 124 ×109/L (150–400) Serum creatinine 139 μmol/L (60–110) Serum ALT 75 U/L (5–35) Serum creatine kinase 455 U/L (24–195) Malaria film x3 negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis This is a classic case of leptospirosis, given the conjunctival suffusion, calf and paraspinal muscle tenderness, and elevated creatine kinase. Contaminated floodwater in urban rodent-infested slums is the likely route of exposure to the leptospires. The clinical manifestations are highly variable, with many subclinical while a few are severe and potentially fatal. Conjunctival suffusion is useful in distinguishing leptospirosis from other common causes of fever.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q44

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man attended the out of hours medical service and asked about postexposure prophylaxis for leptospirosis. He had fallen into a canal earlier that day, and had been fully submerged. He was taking isotretinoin for acne but was not on any other regular medication. He had no known drug allergies. He had no open grazes and had showered 1 hour after the incident.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate postexposure prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: No prophylaxis required The role of postexposure prophylaxis for leptospirosis is debatable, with local guidelines varying. Current UK guidelines are that postexposure management is limited to advice on showering promptly after water exposure, to minimize the swallowing of water, and to thoroughly clean abrasions caused during the water exposure. The contraindication to doxycycline in this patient due to his isotretinoin treatment means that the most appropriate option is no antimicrobial prophylaxis but heightened awareness and self-monitoring for fever and flu-like symptoms.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q49

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presented with fatigue, malaise, abdominal pain, conjunctivitis, and myalgia. He had returned home 4 days earlier from a triathlon event in Hawaii. The myalgia was worse in his calves which he attributed to being sore after the race. In addition to participating in the triathlon, he also reported eating local food and had one unprotected sexual encounter with a fellow female athlete. Investigations: ALT 600 IU/L Bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis The clinical picture is most consistent with leptospirosis, given his exposure to animal-contaminated water in Hawaii and constellation of symptoms, including calf pain, conjunctivitis, abdominal pain, and lab findings.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q11

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents to hospital with critical illness after returning from a trip to Hawaii, where he spent a large amount of time swimming in a lake next to his resort following heavy rains. At presentation he has fever, malaise, and jaundice. The following day he develops acute respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary hemorrhage, and non-oliguric renal failure. Blood cultures, malaria smear, and Dengue serology are negative.
questions.question_raw: A 35 year-old man presents to hospital with critical illness. He recently returned from a trip to Hawaii. He spent a large amount of time swimming in a lake next to his resort after heavy rains. At presentation he has fever, malaise, and jaundice. The following day, he develops acute respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary hemorrhage, and non-oliguric renal failure. Blood cultures, malaria smear, and Dengue serology are negative.

parts.text: What is the most likely condition?
What is the most common natural reservoir for this organism?
List TWO tests that should be ordered at this stage of infection.
What medication should be used for treatment (include dose and route)?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely condition?
What is the most common natural reservoir for this organism?
List TWO tests that should be ordered at this stage of infection.
What medication should be used for treatment (include dose and route)?

questions.model_answer:
a) Severe leptospirosis (Weil disease / severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome due to Leptospira interrogans) — freshwater immersion after heavy rainfall in Hawaii (highest US incidence) with jaundice, ARDS/pulmonary hemorrhage, and non-oliguric renal failure is classic.
b) Rodents and other small mammals are the most important reservoirs (leptospirosis is maintained by chronic renal carriage, with shedding in urine); livestock and companion animals are also significant sources.
c) In this early/acute leptospiremic presentation: (1) Real-time PCR of blood/serum (or urine) — confirms diagnosis during the acute phase before IgM appears; (2) Blood culture in appropriate medium (leptospires recoverable from blood and CSF during the first ~10 days). Acute-phase serum should also be drawn for serology (MAT/IgM-ELISA) with a convalescent sample, though serology is typically negative this early.
d) Moderate-to-severe disease: intravenous penicillin G 1.5 million units IV q6h (ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h is an equally effective alternative).

questions.question: Name the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.
questions.question_raw: What are the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.

parts.text: Laceration that occurs in a lake.
Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash.
A person competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high liver enzymes, and conjunctival suffusion.

parts_raw.text: Laceration that occurs in a lake
Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash
Guy competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high LFTs and conjunctival suffusion

questions.model_answer: a) Streptococcus pneumoniae (leading cause of cochlear implant-associated meningitis; also Haemophilus influenzae). b) Aeromonas hydrophila (also Pseudomonas aeruginosa; freshwater exposure). c) Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat-bite fever; Spirillum minus in Asia). d) Leptospira species (leptospirosis) — fever, elevated LFTs, and conjunctival suffusion after freshwater exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rat-bite (part c) organism is from this chapter; cochlear implant, freshwater laceration, and leptospirosis organisms are from established Mandell/IDSA knowledge in other chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Cochlear implants: meningitis most commonly S. pneumoniae, less often H. influenzae; localized wound infection most commonly S. aureus (also CoNS, streptococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Achromobacter xylosoxidans, Candida albicans); mastoiditis most commonly S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus, Pseudomonas spp, H. influenzae. Lake laceration (fresh/brackish water): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aeromonas hydrophila, Chromobacterium violaceum (immunosuppression/CGD), Mycobacterium fortuitum, Plesiomonas shigelloides, Edwardsiella tarda, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Streptococcus iniae (fish preparation); salt water: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (fish preparation), Mycobacterium marinum, Shewanella spp, Vibrio vulnificus. Rat bite: Streptobacillus moniliformis (most US cases); Spirillum minus (Asia). Triathlon South America: Leptospirosis - abrupt fever, rigors, myalgias, headache after incubation 2-26 days (average 10); conjunctival suffusion important but often overlooked sign (~55% of patients), uncommon in other diseases; subconjunctival hemorrhages also occur.

questions.question: A teenage/young adult man travels to Hawaii with up-to-date pre-travel vaccinations and prophylaxis. He spends a lot of time swimming in a lake on a resort after a large rainfall. He now presents with fever, myalgias, and jaundice. Routine blood cultures, malaria smears, and Dengue serology are all negative. He then develops non-oliguric acute kidney injury and pulmonary hemorrhage.
questions.question_raw: Man/teenager goes to Hawaii and has a great time. He is actually responsible and had all the recommended pre-travel vaccinations and took his prophylaxis as directed, good for him! He spends a lot of time swimming in a lake on a resort after a large rainfall. He now presents with fever, myalgias, jaundice (I don't think they mentioned conjunctival suffusion). Routine blood cultures, malaria smears, and Dengue serology are all negative. He then develops non-oliguric AKI and pulmonary hemorrhage.

parts.text: Name two microbiologic tests you could do at this stage of the infection to confirm the diagnosis.
Name the empiric drug, dose, and route you would recommend.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 microbiologic tests you could do at this stage of the infection to confirm
Name the empiric drug, dose, and route you would recommend.

questions.model_answer:
a) Leptospirosis (severe/Weil disease due to Leptospira interrogans) following freshwater immersion after heavy rainfall.
b) Leptospirosis has no arthropod vector; transmission is via direct or indirect contact with the urine of infected carrier animals. The principal source/reservoir is rodents and other small mammals (livestock and companion animals also contribute).
c) At this acute leptospiremic stage: (1) Real-time PCR on blood/serum (or urine), which confirms infection before seroconversion; (2) Blood culture (leptospires isolable from blood/CSF within the first ~10 days). Paired acute and convalescent serology (MAT, the reference standard, or IgM-ELISA) should also be sent, with a fourfold MAT titer rise confirming the diagnosis.
d) Intravenous penicillin G 1.5 million units IV q6h (alternative: ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h).

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Leptospirosis. Vector/reservoirs: Rodents are the most important reservoirs, but also domestic cattle, swine, dogs, horses, sheep and goats. Tests: Blood for PCR and serology (4-fold rise in titers at 7-14d); Blood culture if available; Urine for PCR (culture if available, valuable beyond 1 week of onset symptoms); CSF PCR if meningitis. Empiric treatment: Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily x7 days; PenG 1.5MU IV q6h x7 days; Doxy as alternative for mild disease; Azithro if pregnant
